front: 150 mM NaCl has an osmolarity of about {{c1::300}} mOsm/L (van 't Hoff factor 2), roughly isotonic to plasma.
why: Osmolarity from molarity times van 't Hoff factor is calculated on essentially every exam

front: A cell rests at Vm = -70 mV and has $E_{Cl} = -70$ mV. What is the net Cl- flux through open Cl- channels?
why: Driving force Vm - E_ion = 0 meaning no net flux is standard neuro reasoning

front: A drug that blocks a cardiac K+ channel prolongs the QT interval. Which phase is affected, and why is that dangerous?
why: Cardiac phase 3 / torsades is clinical detail outside this topic

front: A patient with dilute urine fails to concentrate it after desmopressin. Is the lesion central or nephrogenic, and where does it sit?
why: Central vs nephrogenic DI is clinical flavor of the ADH/AQP2 card

front: An open ion channel passes about {{c1::$10^{7}$}} ions per second, while a carrier turns over only about {{c2::$10^{3}$}} solutes per second.
why: Exact ion/s turnover numbers are trivia; channel-vs-carrier idea covered by kinetics card

front: ATP-dependent {{c1::flippases}} keep phosphatidylserine on the inner leaflet; in apoptosis a Ca2+-activated {{c2::scramblase}} exposes it outward.
why: Flippase/scramblase asymmetry is passage context, secondary

front: Bartter syndrome mimics a {{c1::loop}} diuretic by disabling NKCC2; Gitelman mimics a {{c2::thiazide}} by disabling the distal NaCl cotransporter.
why: Bartter/Gitelman are named renal syndromes; USMLE-level, not AAMC

front: Cholera causes massive watery diarrhea, yet oral rehydration solution containing glucose and salt works. What transport logic explains both?
why: Cholera plus oral rehydration is the classic applied SGLT1 passage scenario

front: Cholesterol buffers fluidity: above the transition temperature it {{c1::decreases}} fluidity, and below it, it {{c2::prevents tight packing}}.
why: Cholesterol's dual effect on fluidity is tested every year

front: Compare SGLT1 and SGLT2 in stoichiometry, location, and clinical relevance.
why: SGLT1 vs SGLT2 stoichiometry/percentages/drugs is trivia; SGLT1 core covered elsewhere

front: Contrast simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion, and active transport.
why: Simple vs facilitated vs active transport is the foundational distinction

front: Define the driving force on an ion and use it to predict Ca2+ movement through an open channel at rest.
why: Driving force definition and predicting ion movement is required neuro reasoning

front: Depolarization means Vm becomes {{c1::less negative}}; opening Cl- channels near rest mainly {{c2::stabilizes}} Vm rather than changing it.
why: Depolarization definition is core; Cl- shunting is a common neuro reasoning point

front: Describe the fluid mosaic model.
why: Fluid mosaic model is foundational membrane content tested every administration

front: Distinguish P-type, V-type, and F-type ATPases with an example of each.
why: P/V/F ATPase classification is prep-book machinery a time-pressed student can skip

front: Distinguish primary and secondary active transport.
why: Primary vs secondary active transport is tested every year

front: During oxidative phosphorylation, the final electron acceptor in the electron transport chain is:
why: O2 as final electron acceptor is tested every administration

front: Fusing a mouse and a human cell gave a heterokaryon whose labeled surface proteins fully intermixed within about {{c1::40 minutes}}.
why: Frye-Edidin named experiment and 40-minute figure are discovery history

front: Gastric parietal cells secrete acid with the {{c1::H+/K+ ATPase}}, a P-type primary pump and the target of proton pump inhibitors.
why: Gastric H+/K+ ATPase as a primary pump is a commonly tested digestive example

front: GLUT{{c1::4}} is the insulin-responsive transporter of muscle and adipose; GLUT{{c2::2}} is the high-Km glucose sensor of liver and pancreatic beta cells.
why: GLUT4 insulin-responsive vs GLUT2 sensor is a yearly discrete

front: How do endocytosis and exocytosis differ?
why: Endocytosis vs exocytosis is core on every administration

front: How do ionophores like valinomycin and uncouplers like DNP dissipate gradients differently?
why: DNP uncoupling and ionophores are frequent ETC/membrane passage content

front: How do the kinetics of carrier-mediated (facilitated) transport differ from simple diffusion?
why: Saturable carrier kinetics vs linear diffusion is a perennial graph question

front: How does the $Na^{+}/K^{+}$ ATPase work?
why: Na+/K+ ATPase 3:2 electrogenic pump is the single most tested transporter

front: How does the thyroid concentrate iodide?
why: NIS iodide symport is a second-tier secondary active transport example

front: Hyperkalemia {{c1::depolarizes}} the resting membrane because raising extracellular K+ makes $E_{K}$ {{c2::less negative}}.
why: Hyperkalemia depolarizing via E_K is classic Nernst reasoning

front: In a FRAP experiment the bleached spot recovers only 60 percent of its fluorescence. What does the missing 40 percent represent?
why: FRAP mobile fraction is experimental-passage reasoning, secondary

front: In Goldman (GHK) terms, what happens to Vm when ACh opens nicotinic channels permeable to both Na+ and K+?
why: GHK weighted-permeability at the end plate is second-step reasoning

front: In the renal collecting duct, {{c1::vasopressin (ADH)}} raises water permeability by driving {{c2::aquaporin-2}} insertion into the apical membrane.
why: ADH driving AQP2 insertion is a commonly tested hormone-transport mechanism

front: Integral membrane proteins are characterized by:
why: Integral vs peripheral membrane proteins is foundational

front: Liddle syndrome is a gain-of-function mutation of the epithelial Na+ channel {{c1::ENaC}}, giving hypertension, hypokalemia, and {{c2::low}} aldosterone.
why: Liddle syndrome is a named clinical syndrome; trivia for MCAT

front: Lipid rafts are ordered microdomains enriched in {{c1::cholesterol and sphingolipids}} that concentrate particular receptors and GPI-anchored proteins.
why: Lipid rafts are supporting detail on membrane organization

front: Osmolarity differs from tonicity because tonicity considers:
why: Tonicity counting only non-penetrating solutes is tested every year

front: Osmotic pressure is colligative. What does $\pi = iMRT$ imply when comparing solutions across a membrane?
why: Applying pi = iMRT to compare solutions is a standard calculation

front: Predict red cell shape in 100 mM NaCl versus 400 mM NaCl, and name each response.
why: Worked RBC tonicity example supports the plainer hypertonic/hypotonic card

front: Rank O2, water, glucose, and Na+ by permeability through a pure lipid bilayer, and state what sets the order.
why: Ranking bilayer permeability by size, polarity and charge appears every year

front: Resting membrane potential lies closest to $E_{K}$ because the resting membrane is most permeable to {{c1::K+}} through leak channels.
why: Resting potential near E_K from K+ leak is tested every administration

front: SGLT1 moves glucose {{c1::against}} its gradient by coupling it to {{c2::Na+}} flowing downhill — apical membrane of intestine and proximal tubule.
why: SGLT1 Na+-coupled uphill glucose is the canonical secondary active example

front: Single-channel patch clamp shows square, all-or-none current steps rather than a smoothly graded current. What does that reveal?
why: Single-channel patch clamp interpretation is passage technique, secondary

front: The endosymbiotic theory proposes that mitochondria evolved from:
why: Endosymbiotic origin of mitochondria is tested every year

front: The glycocalyx functions in:
why: Glycocalyx function is definition-level, occasionally asked

front: The Na+/H+ exchanger (NHE) is an electroneutral antiporter regulating intracellular {{c1::pH}} and reabsorbing Na+ in the {{c2::proximal tubule}}.
why: NHE antiporter is a second-tier example with renal context

front: The Na+/K+ ATPase consumes roughly {{c1::20-30 percent}} of a typical cell's ATP, and as much as {{c2::70 percent}} in neurons.
why: Percent-of-ATP figures are exact numbers not on the AAMC outline

front: The thick ascending limb reabsorbs salt via the {{c1::Na+-K+-2Cl- (NKCC2)}} symporter, target of {{c2::loop}} diuretics.
why: NKCC2 and loop diuretics are renal passage context, secondary

front: Trace transcellular glucose absorption across an enterocyte, naming the transporter and energetics at each membrane.
why: Transcellular glucose absorption with polarized transporters is a classic question

front: Transporter classes: {{c1::uniporters}} move one solute (GLUT1); {{c2::symporters}} couple two in the same direction (SGLT1); antiporters swap them (NCX).
why: Uniport/symport/antiport with canonical examples is core vocabulary tested every year

front: Two membranes share head groups but differ in melting behavior. Which acyl chain features predict the more fluid one?
why: Unsaturation and chain length setting fluidity is tested every administration

front: Typical gradients: K+ is about {{c1::140}} mM inside versus 4 mM outside, while Na+ is about 145 mM outside versus {{c2::12}} mM inside.
why: Typical K+ and Na+ gradients are needed as given values in Nernst-style problems

front: Typical neuronal equilibrium potentials: $E_{K} \approx$ {{c1::-90}} mV and $E_{Na} \approx$ {{c2::+60}} mV.
why: E_K and E_Na values are used constantly in neuro questions

front: What are tight junctions, desmosomes, and gap junctions?
why: Tight, desmosome and gap junction roles are tested every year

front: What distinguishes primary from secondary active transport? Give an example of each.
why: Examples for primary/secondary transport are supporting detail on the core card

front: What do ABC transporters do? Name two medically important members with different mechanisms.
why: ABC transporters and CFTR appear in passages as supplied context

front: What happens to a cell in hypertonic vs. hypotonic solution?
why: Cell response to hypertonic vs hypotonic solution is core every year

front: What is osmotic pressure?
why: Osmotic pressure definition and pi = iMRT is foundational

front: What is the chloride shift, and which transporter performs it?
why: Chloride shift via Cl-/HCO3- exchange is tested CO2-transport content

front: What is transcytosis, and where is it physiologically important?
why: Transcytosis definition is useful for understanding; FcRn detail is secondary

front: What makes a transporter electrogenic versus electroneutral? Classify NCX, NHE, and AE1.
why: Electrogenic vs electroneutral classification is second-step reasoning

front: Which describes secondary active transport?
why: Near-restatement of the primary/secondary and SGLT1 cards

front: Which membrane is impermeable to most ions, creating the proton gradient?
why: Inner mitochondrial membrane impermeability drives the proton gradient; tested every year

front: Why do red blood cells and the blood-brain barrier rely on GLUT1?
why: GLUT1 low-Km reasoning supports the GLUT distinction card

front: Why do severe liver disease and nephrotic syndrome cause edema, in Starling terms?
why: Starling oncotic pressure and edema is commonly tested cardiovascular reasoning

front: Why does a tenfold Ca2+ gradient produce only about 30 mV of equilibrium potential while the same Na+ gradient gives about 61 mV?
why: Nernst valence term is second-step calculation reasoning

front: Why does inhibiting the Na+/K+ ATPase eventually make cells swell and lyse?
why: Pump inhibition causing swelling is a common Na+/K+ ATPase reasoning question

front: Why does ouabain poisoning stop secondary active transport, even though those transporters use no ATP?
why: Ouabain collapsing the Na+ gradient for all coupled transport is classic reasoning

front: Why is 300 mM urea isosmotic yet hypotonic to a red blood cell?
why: Urea isosmotic yet hypotonic is the canonical tonicity question

front: Why is sweat chloride high in cystic fibrosis when CFTR failure elsewhere produces thick, dehydrated secretions?
why: CF sweat vs airway direction is clinical flavor
